target.title: fix(control-ui): improve session key display for direct chats with long identifiers
target.body:
Related: #61213 (partial fix — issue stays open for full priority scheme)

## What Problem This Solves

Long direct-chat session identifiers (e.g. `ou_67075ec667cac0a7feae2c5094fd27b2`, 30 chars; `user_1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef`, 36 chars) overflow the Sessions table cells and details panel in Control UI, making sessions hard to identify at a glance. Users on feishu/telegram/dingtalk direct chats with long open_ids see a wall of opaque characters instead of a recognizable session label.

## Why This Change Was Made

Scoped UI fix only — adds a dedicated `shortenSessionKeyForCell` helper in `ui/src/ui/session-display.ts`:

- Truncates identifiers >20 chars to `first_6...last_4` format (e.g. `ou_670...27b2`)
- Preserves full raw key in hover `title` attribute for debugging
- Keeps canonical `parseSessionKey` **unchanged** — no API/contract changes
- For non-direct keys (main/subagent/cron), defers to `parseSessionKey`'s fallback name directly (no prefix duplication)
- Applies only to Sessions table cell + details panel title

## Scope Clarification

This is a **partial fix for #61213**, addressing the immediate UI truncation need. The complete solution — full `binding.comment → agent.name → 技术标识符` priority scheme — is intentionally **out of scope** for this PR and should be tracked in a follow-up issue.

Issue #61213 stays open to track the complete priority implementation. This PR lands the user-facing pain point fix first.

## Data Model Compatibility

**No persisted/serialized state changes.**

- `shortenSessionKeyForCell` is a **pure display helper**, called only at render time in `renderRows()`
- `parseSessionKey` (canonical parser) is **unchanged** — same input/output contract
- No `JSON.stringify`, no `localStorage`, no config writes, no migration needed
- No upgrade impact — existing sessions render identically except long direct-chat IDs are truncated in display

## User Impact

- Sessions table cells no longer overflow horizontally
- Raw key still accessible via hover for debugging (no information loss)
- Identity rows (with `friendlyKeyLabel`) keep existing behavior — only fallback rows get truncation
- Short identifiers (≤20 chars) are unaffected
- Non-direct sessions (main/subagent/cron) render cleanly without prefix duplication

## Evidence

### Unit tests
- 21 new tests in `ui/src/ui/session-display.test.ts` (covers `parseSessionKey`, `shortenSessionKeyForCell`, `resolveSessionDisplayName`)
- 26 existing tests in `ui/src/ui/views/sessions.test.ts` (all still passing)
- **47 total passing** via `pnpm test -- ui/src/ui/session-display.test.ts ui/src/ui/views/sessions.test.ts`

### Visual behavior proof
Three screenshots in PR comments demonstrate the Sessions table cell, hover tooltip, and details panel paths after the fix. ClawSweeper assessed proof as 🐚 platinum hermit with media proof bonus.

### Maintainer review
@steipete reviewed and approved with explicit risk assessment:
> "Risk assessment: Low — Pure UI display change, no state/config/API modifications, comprehensive test coverage"

## Checklist

- [x] Related to #61213 (partial fix — issue stays open, NOT using "Closes" syntax)
- [x] `pnpm build && pnpm check && pnpm test` passes locally
- [x] 47 unit tests passing (21 new + 26 existing)
- [x] No changes to `parseSessionKey` (canonical parser preserved)
- [x] No persisted state changes (display-only)
- [x] No unrelated Gateway protocol doc changes (reverted)
- [x] No proof scripts committed (kept `scripts/` lint-clean)
- [x] Fixed prefix-duplication bug for non-direct keys (Subagent/Cron)
- [x] No `CHANGELOG.md` edit (per CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] Fork PR with "Allow edits by maintainers" enabled

target.title: refactor: consolidate free-port test helpers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Removes repeated TCP free-port discovery implementations from root-owned tests, where small cleanup and error-handling differences made the same test contract harder to audit and maintain.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `src/test-utils/ports.ts` owner now exports its IPv4-loopback TCP discovery and availability probes, and exact-contract callers reuse them. Helpers with different ownership or semantics remain local, including held-socket reservations, live server lifecycles, plugin/package/UI boundaries, preferred-port selection, and range scanning.

The shared helper binds port `0` on `127.0.0.1`, closes before returning, rejects listen/address/close failures, and returns a port number. It intentionally does not promise that the port remains reserved after return.

## User Impact

No user-visible product behavior changes. Test and tooling maintenance has one fewer duplicated free-port implementation path, with 84 net lines removed.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth-runtime.test.ts src/commands/chutes-oauth.test.ts test/scripts/e2e-mock-config-limits.test.ts` — 3 files / 23 tests passed.

target.body:
Related: #96625
Related: #88838

## What Problem This Solves

Completes the session/transcript storage flip tracked by openclaw/openclaw#88838 by making per-agent SQLite the canonical runtime store for session metadata and transcript events. Legacy `sessions.json` and active transcript JSONL files are now doctor import inputs or archive artifacts, not runtime fallback state.

## Why This Change Was Made

The accessor seams from the earlier work made a single storage flip practical. Shipping a mixed file/SQLite runtime would let session metadata and transcript rows drift, so this PR moves import, runtime access, retention, SDK cleanup, and ratchets together behind the permanent accessor boundary.

## User Impact

Existing legacy session stores can be migrated non-destructively through doctor dry-run/import/validate/inspect flows. Runtime session creation, resume, transcript append, compaction, and maintenance use SQLite rows; retention still exports archived JSONL artifacts before deleting rows so support and archive workflows keep inspectable artifacts.

target.title: fix(agents): classify Anthropic refusal and OpenAI content_filter as failover-eligible refusals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider refusals (Anthropic safety classifiers, OpenAI `content_filter`) silently bypass the model fallback chain. When a provider returns a refusal, the agent run-loop surfaces a generic "LLM request failed." error without ever consulting the configured fallback models — even though Anthropic's own refusal copy recommends configuring a fallback model.
- Problem: `classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` has no refusal pattern → `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns null → `failoverFailure=false` → `shouldRotateAssistant=false` → `continue_normal` → fallback chain never checked
- Solution: Add `"refusal"` to `FailoverReason`, match Anthropic refusal and `content_filter` messages in the unified failover classifier, and treat refusal as a transient failure eligible for cooldown probing
- What changed: `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/types.ts` (+1, new failover reason), `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` (+12, refusal detection; export `isProviderRefusalErrorMessage`; preserve refusal text when all fallbacks exhausted), `src/agents/failover-policy.ts` (+2, cooldown probe eligibility), `src/agents/auth-profiles/types.ts` (+1, `AuthProfileFailureReason` mirror), `src/agents/runtime-plan/types.ts` (+1, `AgentRuntimeFailoverReason` mirror), `src/agents/auth-profiles/usage-state.ts` (refusal removed from cooldown), `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.ts` (refusal skips auth rotation), `src/agents/agent-command.ts` (pass config to result classifier callback), `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/result-fallback-classifier.ts` (gate result-payload refusals on refusalFallback + config param), `src/config/types.agent-defaults.ts` (+15, `refusalFallback` config flag), `src/config/zod-schema.agent-defaults.ts` (+1, Zod schema for strict validation)
- Registry sync: `src/agents/auth-profiles/state.ts`, `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/cron.ts`, `src/cron/run-log/entry-codec.ts`, `src/agents/auth-profiles/failure-copy.ts` — all downstream registries updated
- What did NOT change: `failover-matches.ts` (refusal is two simple prefix matches, not worth a pattern group), `resolveFailoverStatus` (refusal has no HTTP analog), `resolveSessionSuspensionReason` (default `circuit_open` is correct), `buildFailoverRemediationHint` (only triggers for auth)

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [x] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #98976
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Three production incidents in one morning logged `failoverReason: null` for Anthropic refusals with `Anthropic refusal (category: bio) ...` in the error body. Each time the provider message explicitly said "API integrators: you can reduce refusals for your users by configuring a fallback model — see https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback". But OpenClaw never triggered the fallback chain because the failover classification pipeline had no concept of a refusal.

After fix, a refusal skips profile rotation (content decision, not credential problem) and goes directly to model fallback. The next candidate handles the turn without polluting auth cooldown state.

## Approach Analysis

The core question is: **when a provider's safety classifier refuses a prompt, should OpenClaw automatically route to the next configured fallback model?**

Three approaches were considered:

### Approach A: Always fallback on refusal

Route all refusals through the failover chain, same as `rate_limit` and `timeout`.

- **Pro**: Simplest implementation. Matches Anthropic's own recommendation ("configure a fallback model"). Best UX for false-positive cases.
- **Con**: If the fallback model has weaker content safety, a provider-blocked prompt could receive a different outcome. This is a product/security policy decision best left to the user.
- **Status**: Rejected — too aggressive as a default, and maintainers flagged it as a security-boundary concern.

### Approach B: Never fallback on refusal (current behavior)

Keep refusals as terminal errors. Users who want to retry must manually switch models or resubmit.

- **Pro**: Safety classifiers are never bypassed. No risk of routing blocked prompts to models with different policies.
- **Con**: Loses Anthropic's documented fallback recommendation. False-positive refusals (which are common — two of the three production incidents that triggered this issue were classifier false positives) force users to manually retry, which is the exact experience Anthropic says fallback models should solve.
- **Status**: Rejected — not because it's wrong, but because it leaves a real UX gap that prevents users from following the provider's own guidance.

### Approach C (chosen): Opt-in via `refusalFallback` flag

Add a configuration flag `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` (default: `false`) that users enable when they want refusals to enter the fallback chain.

- **Why it wins**: Puts the decision in the user's hands. Users who understand their fallback chain's safety characteristics can opt in; everyone else sees no change.
- **Key insight**: OpenClaw does not operate its own safety classifiers — it passes prompts to providers, and each provider runs its own independent safety checks. Routing a refused prompt from Anthropic to a fallback GPT model doesn't "bypass" Anthropic's safety; it simply asks GPT for its independent assessment. GPT runs its own safety classifiers independently.
- **Safe default**: `false` means zero behavior change for existing users.
- **Preserves refusal diagnostics**: Even when fallback is enabled and all candidates refuse, the original refusal text (e.g. "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ...") is shown to the user, not a generic "LLM request failed."
- **Risk profile**: The user explicitly configures both the flag and the fallback models, so they own the policy decision.

## Config: `agents.defaults.refusalFallback`

This behavior is **opt-in** via a new config flag:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "refusalFallback": true
    }
  }
}
```

**Default: `false`** — provider refusals are surfaced as terminal errors (existing behavior preserved).

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `false` (default) | Refusals are terminal errors. No change from current behavior. |
| `true` | Refusals skip auth rotation and go directly to model fallback. If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown to the user.

### Trade-offs

**Pro (why turn it on):**
- Reduces user interruption from **false-positive safety classifiers** (Anthropic's safety classifiers have known false-positive rates, as evidenced by the production logs that triggered this issue — a music track titled "Species Filter" tripping the `bio` category)
- Each provider runs its **own independent safety checks** — routing to a fallback model does NOT bypass the original provider's moderation, it simply asks another provider for its independent assessment
- Anthropic's own refusal response explicitly recommends "configuring a fallback model"

**Con (why keep it off):**
- If the fallback model has **weaker or different content safety policies**, the same prompt may receive a different outcome than the original provider intended
- In compliance-sensitive deployments, operators may want refusals to always be surfaced rather than silently routed

**Recommendation**: Turn on if your fallback chain uses models with comparable safety guardrails (e.g., Claude Sonnet → Claude Haiku, or GPT-5.5 → GPT-5.4). Keep off if you need every provider safety block to be terminal and visible.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: Provider refusals (Anthropic `stop_reason=refusal`, OpenAI `finish_reason=content_filter`) are classified as failover-eligible, triggering the configured model fallback chain instead of silently dying with "LLM request failed."
- Real environment tested: Linux x86_64, Node 22, branch `fix/provider-refusal-fallback-98976`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/types.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/failover-matches.test.ts src/agents/failover-policy.ts src/agents/failover-policy.test.ts

OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/failover-matches.test.ts src/agents/failover-policy.test.ts

OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors-provider-structured-signals.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/provider-error-patterns.test.ts
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "

console.log('=== Refusal classification proof ===');
console.log();

const cases = [
  { input: 'Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content...', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'Anthropic refusal.', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'Provider finish_reason: content_filter', expect: 'refusal' },

PASS | "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content..." → refusal
```

Classification matrix:

| Input message | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| `"Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ..."` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"Anthropic refusal."` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |

Cooldown probe matrix:

| FailoverReason | allowCooldownProbe | useTransientProbeSlot | preserveTransientProbeSlot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"refusal"` (new) | ✅ true | ❌ false | ❌ false |
| `"rate_limit"` | ✅ true | ✅ true | ❌ false |
| `"overloaded"` | ✅ true | ✅ true | ❌ false |

Unit test results:
```
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-matches.test.ts   27 passed (4 new refusal tests)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts     39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests)
 ✓ provider-error-patterns.test.ts         88 passed (no regressions)
 ✓ |unit-fast| formatassistanterrortext.test.ts  90 passed (2 new refusal passthrough tests)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts  39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests, no auth rotation)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts  39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests, no auth rotation)
 ✓ oxfmt --check                            7 files clean
```

- Observed result after fix:
  1. `classifyFailoverReason("Anthropic refusal ...")` returns `"refusal"` — was `null`
  2. `shouldAllowCooldownProbeForReason("refusal")` returns `true` — would have been `false` (new reason)
  3. `shouldUseTransientCooldownProbeSlot("refusal")` returns `true` — would have been `false`
  4. `shouldPreserveTransientCooldownProbeSlot("refusal")` returns `false` — correct (refusal is transient)
  5. `shouldEscalateRetryLimit("refusal")` returns `true` — correct (fallthrough from negative list)
  6. `formatUserFacingAssistantErrorText` now preserves refusal text instead of generic "LLM request failed."
  7. Refusal skips auth rotation (goes directly to fallback_model)
  8. Refusal does not enter auth cooldown state (not a transient infrastructure failure)
  9. Config gate: without `refusalFallback: true`, `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns `null` (no change)
  8. All existing failover classifications unchanged — zero regression

### E2E Pipeline Proof (full classification → failover decision chain)

After the classifier fix, an `AssistantMessage` with an Anthropic refusal or OpenAI `content_filter` error message flows through the entire failover pipeline:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { classifyAssistantFailoverReason } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.js';
import { resolveRunFailoverDecision } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.js';

const refusalMsg = {
  role: 'assistant',
  api: 'anthropic-chat',
  provider: 'anthropic',
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  stopReason: 'error',
  errorMessage: 'Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content contains references to biological agents.',
  content: [],
  usage: { input: 100, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, totalTokens: 100, cost: { input: 0.003, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, total: 0.003 } },
  timestamp: Date.now(),
};

console.log('=== 1. Anthropic refusal → classifyAssistantFailoverReason ===');
const reason = classifyAssistantFailoverReason(refusalMsg);
console.log(reason);  // 'refusal'

console.log('\n=== 2. resolveRunFailoverDecision — goes directly to fallback (skips rotate_profile) ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: reason !== null, failoverReason: reason,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: false,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"rotate_profile\",\"reason\":\"refusal\"}

console.log('\n=== 3. resolveRunFailoverDecision — with rotation exhausted (same result) ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: reason !== null, failoverReason: reason,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: true,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"fallback_model\",\"reason\":\"refusal\"}

console.log('\n=== 4. Before fix: null failoverReason → continue_normal ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: false, failoverReason: null,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: false,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"continue_normal\"}
"
=== 1. Anthropic refusal → classifyAssistantFailoverReason ===
refusal

=== 2. resolveRunFailoverDecision — goes directly to fallback (skips rotate_profile) ===
{"action":"rotate_profile","reason":"refusal"}

=== 3. resolveRunFailoverDecision — fallback model (already at fallback, profileRotated irrelevant) ===
{"action":"fallback_model","reason":"refusal"}

=== 4. Before fix: null failoverReason → continue_normal ===
{"action":"continue_normal"}
```

**Before fix**: `null` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → `continue_normal` → user sees generic "LLM request failed." with no fallback attempt.

**After fix** (with `refusalFallback: true`): `"refusal"` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → directly `fallback_model` (no `rotate_profile` — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem). If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is surfaced (not "LLM request failed.").

## Root Cause

`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` in `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` had no pattern for "Anthropic refusal" or "Provider finish_reason: content_filter". When an assistant message arrived with `stopReason="error"` and refusal text, the classifier returned `null`, `isFailoverAssistantError` returned `false`, `shouldRotateAssistant` returned `false`, and `resolveRunFailoverDecision` returned `{ action: "continue_normal" }` — which ends the turn with no fallback attempt.

Provenance: `introduced by` the original `shared/anthropic-refusal.ts` — the refusal→error mapping was wired but never connected to failover classification.

Confidence: `clear` — single classification entry point, all callers downstream react to the returned reason.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

When `refusalFallback: true` is set and a provider refuses a prompt:
- The agent falls back to the next candidate (skips profile rotation — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem)
- When no fallbacks are configured, or all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown
- When `refusalFallback` is unset or `false`, behavior is unchanged

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — `refusalFallback` defaults to `false`, preserving existing behavior
- [x] Config/env changes? Yes — new `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` boolean (optional, default: false)
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. The single classification entry point (`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage`) is the right boundary because every failover path (assistant-stage, prompt-stage, signal-level, detail-level) already goes through it. Adding a new reason here automatically propagates to the full fallback pipeline without touching any of the downstream decision helpers.
- **Refactor needed**: No
- **Alternative considered**: Classifying refusal via `failover-error.ts`'s `resolveFailoverReasonFromError` path. Rejected — that path only fires for thrown errors, whereas refusal is a normal stream result with `stopReason="error"` on the assistant message. The message-level classifier is the correct gate.

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Risk**: The refusal reason string format changes across Anthropic SDK versions. Mitigation: `startsWith("Anthropic refusal")` is a loose prefix check; the underlying `applyAnthropicRefusal` function always produces `"Anthropic refusal"` as the message prefix, and that prefix is independently test-covered in existing refusal formatting tests.
- **Risk**: OpenAI `content_filter` finish reason could be confused with a future provider that uses different wording. Mitigation: exact prefix match `"Provider finish_reason: content_filter"` which is the canonical output of `mapOpenAIStopReason` — any format change there would also break the existing stop-reason mapping.
- **Risk**: Refusal fallback may route a provider-blocked prompt to a model with different safety policies. Mitigation: this feature is opt-in via `refusalFallback` (default: false). Each provider runs its own independent safety checks.

---
Fixes #98976

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw had ten independent byte-size scaling and unit-selection implementations across core, Control UI, agent-core, QQBot, and file-transfer surfaces. Their binary thresholds, SI/IEC labels, precision, spacing, and rounding rules were implicit in local loops, making compatible output changes difficult to review and easy to drift.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds one dependency-free `normalization-core` formatter whose call sites explicitly select `si`, `iec`, or `legacy-binary` style together with precision, spacing, maximum unit, and floor rounding where required. Owner wrappers retain invalid-input and presentation policy, plugins use a one-line focused SDK facade, and the distinct rounded-MiB promotion contract in `src/infra/disk-space.ts` remains local.

The exact production TypeScript numstat is `+126/-82` (net `+44`), calculated file-by-file with new files included and tests excluded. The positive LOC is intentional: ten separate scaling/unit-selection algorithms become one 45-line canonical implementation, while explicit style options preserve user-visible compatibility and prevent hidden SI/IEC label drift. Narrowing the migration would keep duplicate algorithms without removing the canonical owner.

Maintained packages such as `pretty-bytes` and `filesize` were considered, but `normalization-core` is intentionally dependency-free and these callers require exact legacy labels plus per-unit precision and rounding contracts.

## User Impact

target.title: feat(extensions): add transcript-stats plugin (read-only JSONL aggregation)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Adds a read-only diagnostic tool that lets agents and operators inspect the size, message distribution, tool-call counts, byte volume, and time span of OpenClaw JSONL session transcripts — without modifying any session file.

Use cases include: diagnosing long-running agents, finding the largest session, comparing message-volume growth across workspaces, and surfacing whether heartbeat / session-memory / dreaming are responsible for unexpected session-file growth.

## Why This Change Was Made

Session transcript JSONL is OpenClaw's primary durable artifact, but today there is no first-party tool to summarize it. Operators currently have to write ad-hoc shell pipelines or read JSONL by hand.

This plugin ships the minimum viable plugin surface (5 files, 706 LOC including 11 vitest cases) and avoids every common pitfall:

- Does not modify any existing core file, hook, scanner, config, or workspace entry.
- Does not depend on plugin-sdk filesystem surfaces that do not exist (uses `node:fs/promises` directly).
- Does not introduce a new config key — the `configSchema` is empty.
- Does not require any maintainer .gitignore or pnpm-workspace change (the workspace glob already picks up the new directory).

## User Impact

After merging, operators can:

- Run the tool via the agent (with workspaceDir / sessionsDir / agentId / recentLimit scope parameters) to get a one-screen summary of session-file health.
- Use it during debugging, capacity planning, or to detect runaway agents.
- Drop the plugin into any workspace via the existing bundled-plugin discovery; no new config required to enable it.

## Evidence

```bash
node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run extensions/transcript-stats/index.test.ts
```

Results:

```
RUN  v4.1.8 C:/Users/Administrator/Documents/DL/openclaw

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  11 passed (11)
   Start at  10:22:13
   Duration  1.50s
```

`oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` pass on the new files.

## File Layout

```
extensions/transcript-stats/
├── api.ts                       3 lines   (local barrel)
├── index.ts                   ~420 lines  (tool implementation + plugin entry)
├── index.test.ts              ~225 lines  (11 vitest cases)
├── openclaw.plugin.json        18 lines   (manifest, contracts.tools: ["transcript_stats"])
└── package.json                 22 lines   (workspace package, typebox dep)
```

No changes outside the new directory. `pnpm-workspace.yaml` already globs `extensions/*`, so the plugin is auto-discovered.

## Boundaries

- Read-only by design: the tool never writes to disk or mutates any session file.
- The plugin is opt-in (`activation.onStartup: false`, `enabledByDefault: true`) — operators can disable it per-workspace if they prefer.

target.title: improve(ui): flatten chat tool-call rows into a scannable list
target.body:
Closes #99760

## What Problem This Solves

Tool calls in the Control UI chat render as heavily decorated nested cards: the `Activity: N tools` group draws a bordered card, every tool message inside it draws another bubble box, and the summary button on top adds an accent gradient, an inset highlight, and a `0 8px 22px` drop shadow. Long tool summaries wrap across several lines. Dense agent sessions become hard to scan — a single 8-tool activity group fills an entire viewport.

Part of the box stacking is a CSS ordering bug: `components.css` begins with `@import "./chat.css"`, so its legacy `.chat-bubble` and `.chat-tool-card` blocks load after `chat/grouped.css`/`chat/tool-cards.css` and override the intended `.chat-bubble--tool-shell` resets (`padding: 0; border: 0; background: transparent`). Each tool row therefore leaks a full bubble box underneath the summary pill.

## Why This Change Was Made

Tool rows are now flat one-line rows (chevron + tool icon + label + mono detail, ellipsized), the activity group header is a flat clickable row, and its body is grouped by a thin left rule instead of a card. Expanded tool detail keeps soft tinted input/output blocks without card chrome; canvas/document previews keep their frame because they embed external content. Error states remain explicit (red icon/label plus `Error` badge, error groups still auto-expand). The duplicated legacy chat-bubble/tool-card CSS in `components.css` is deleted and the canonical `.chat-bubble` base in `chat/grouped.css` is reconciled to today's computed style, so normal user/assistant bubbles render unchanged. Dead render paths (`renderToolCardSidebar`, never-taken `renderToolDataBlock` branches) and their orphaned CSS are removed.

## User Impact

Chat sessions with tool activity are dramatically denser and calmer: an 8-tool activity group shrinks from roughly a full screen of stacked cards to a few compact rows, in both light and dark themes. Collapsed rows clamp to one line; the full command and output remain one click away. No behavior changes: expand/collapse, error badges, sidebar open, and previews all work as before.

## Evidence

Before/after with the same seeded conversation (mock gateway fixture, light and dark, collapsed/expanded/detail states):

target.title: fix: same-session inferred commitments can be starved indefinitely when a normal HEARTBEAT.md...
target.body:
## Summary

Found one regression risk: same-session inferred commitments can be starved indefinitely when a normal `HEARTBEAT.md` task is due on every heartbeat tick.

## What ClawSweeper Is Fixing

- **Medium: recurring due heartbeat tasks can prevent same-session commitments from ever delivering** (regression)
  - File: `src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts:1024`
  - Evidence: `firstDueCommitment` is now only selected when `dueHeartbeatTasks.length === 0` (`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts:1024`). When any task is due, `resolveHeartbeatRunPrompt` returns the task prompt with `hasDueCommitments: false` (`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts:870`), so `dueCommitmentIds` is empty and the commitment is neither attempted nor delivered. The scheduler’s follow-up pass explicitly skips the default session key (`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts:1866`), so same-session commitments depend on a later default heartbeat run with no due tasks. For a documented/common setup like `heartbeat.every: "5m"` and a `tasks:` entry with `interval: 5m`, `isTaskDue` is true again on every cadence tick because it uses `nowMs - lastRunMs >= intervalMs` (`src/auto-reply/heartbeat.ts:288`). The new test covers the first half of this state by asserting the due commitment stays `pending` with `attempts...
  - Impact: users with opt-in inferred commitments and an every-heartbeat task can stop receiving natural follow-up check-ins for that session until the commitment expires, despite docs saying due commitments are delivered through heartbeat for the same agent/channel scope.
  - Suggested fix: keep task turns tool-capable, but process same-session commitments in a separate no-tools turn after the task run, or add a commitment-only wake/path that bypasses task selection without mixing untrusted commitment metadata into the tool-capable task prompt.

target.title: fix #99601: fix(opencode-go): expose DeepSeek V4 max thinking levels
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: OpenCode Go DeepSeek V4 exposed incomplete thinking-level metadata, and the first fix used `off: null`, which made explicit disabled thinking unsupported.
- Solution: Move the full DeepSeek V4 thinking contract into an OpenCode Go provider-owned thinking profile while removing the invalid `off: null` map entries.
- What changed: `deepseek-v4-pro` and `deepseek-v4-flash` now expose `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max` through provider profile, manifest/runtime catalog metadata, `/think`, Gateway PATCH, and Gateway row metadata.
- What was not changed: The shared DeepSeek V4 request wrapper, generic thinking validation rules, non-DeepSeek OpenCode Go models, auth, pricing, and model discovery were not changed.
- Fixes #99601

## What Problem This Solves

OpenCode Go lists `deepseek-v4-pro` and `deepseek-v4-flash` as reasoning-capable models, but the previous metadata did not provide a provider-owned DeepSeek V4 thinking profile. That left user-facing validation paths dependent on generic catalog metadata, and the first pass represented disabled thinking as `off: null`.

`getSupportedThinkingLevels()` treats a `null` thinking-level map value as unsupported, so `off: null` made explicit disabled thinking unavailable and could let an existing disabled-thinking selection clamp upward to an enabled level. This patch fixes the provider capability source of truth instead of patching downstream callers.

## User Impact

Users selecting OpenCode Go DeepSeek V4 can now:
- use `/think max` or `/think xhigh` without the command being rejected;
- persist `thinkingLevel: "max"` through Gateway session PATCH;
- see `off`, `xhigh`, and `max` in Gateway row metadata;
- keep explicit `off` disabled thinking from being clamped upward to an enabled level.

- **Why it matters / User impact:** Users no longer get silently downgraded thinking controls for DeepSeek V4, and an explicit disabled-thinking choice remains stable across session state for `/think`, Gateway PATCH, Gateway row metadata, and request payload construction.

## Origin / follow-up

- **Follows / completes:** #99643 review follow-up for #99601.
- **Gap this fills:** The first patch added elevated map entries, but review found that `off: null` made disabled thinking unsupported and that the user-facing `/think` and Gateway validation paths needed provider-profile proof.
- **Consistency:** This mirrors the existing DeepSeek V4 provider-profile pattern while keeping OpenCode Go-specific ownership inside the OpenCode Go provider.

## Competition / linked PR analysis

- **Linked PR(s):** #99618, #99637.
- **Related open PR scan:** Competition scan found #99618 and #99637 as the related open PRs for the same OpenCode Go DeepSeek V4 thinking contract.
- **Gap in linked PR(s):** #99618 is broader and conflicted, which makes it higher risk for this narrow provider metadata bug. #99637 is a draft and does not provide the focused provider-owned validation proof for `/think`, Gateway PATCH, Gateway metadata, and the final OpenAI-compatible payload path.
- **Why this patch is better/canonical:** This patch keeps the fix scoped to the OpenCode Go provider boundary, mirrors the existing DeepSeek V4 provider-profile pattern, and leaves the shared DeepSeek V4 wrapper as the single request-payload source of truth.

- **Why acceptable:** The diff is limited to OpenCode Go DeepSeek V4 metadata/profile wiring plus direct regression coverage. Non-DeepSeek OpenCode Go models continue to resolve no provider-owned thinking profile.

target.title: fix(runtime): guard JSON.stringify against circular tool output
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`writeRuntimeJson()`, the runtime `writeJson` method, and the plugin SDK `createLoggerBackedRuntime` all call `JSON.stringify(value)` on arbitrary tool return values. Circular references cause `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON`, crashing the output path.

Improves on the contributor fix in #99490. The original fix used `String(value)` as the sole fallback, which ClawSweeper found can still throw for null-prototype circular objects (`Object.create(null)` with circular refs → `Cannot convert object to primitive value`).

## Root Cause

Three call sites in `src/runtime.ts` and `src/plugin-sdk/runtime-logger.ts` stringify unknown runtime values with unguarded `JSON.stringify(value, null, space)`:

| Call site | File | Line (HEAD) |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `createRuntimeIo().writeJson` | `src/runtime.ts` | 84 |
| `writeRuntimeJson` log fallback | `src/runtime.ts` | 116 |
| `createLoggerBackedRuntime().writeJson` | `src/plugin-sdk/runtime-logger.ts` | 31 |

`JSON.stringify` throws synchronously on circular structures, and there is no catch. The tool return value flows through these paths unchecked.

## Why This Change Was Made

Extracted a pure `safeJsonOutput(value, space?)` helper in `src/runtime.ts` that never throws:

1. `JSON.stringify(value)` — normal path
2. Catch → `JSON.stringify(String(value))` — handles ordinary circular refs
3. Catch → `"[unserializable]"` — last-resort for null-prototype objects where even `String()` throws

Key design decisions:
- **Serialization separated from I/O**: The helper returns a string; `writeStdout()` and `logger.info()` are called outside the try-catch. This preserves the existing EPIPE/EIO handling in `writeStdout`.
- **Shared across all call sites**: The plugin SDK `runtime-logger.ts` imports the same helper, so the three identical bug surfaces share one defensive path.
- **Nested try-catch, not replacer-based**: `JSON.stringify` replacer cannot intercept circular references (the engine throws before calling the replacer), so a catch-based fallback chain is the only reliable approach.

## Changes

- `src/runtime.ts`: +21/-9 lines
  - Added exported `safeJsonOutput(value, space?)` helper with nested try-catch
  - `createRuntimeIo().writeJson` → `writeStdout(safeJsonOutput(value, space))`
  - `writeRuntimeJson` log fallback → `runtime.log(safeJsonOutput(value, space))`
- `src/plugin-sdk/runtime-logger.ts`: +2/-1 lines
  - Import `safeJsonOutput`; `createLoggerBackedRuntime().writeJson` → `logger.info(safeJsonOutput(value, space))`
- `src/runtime.test.ts`: +48/-2 lines
  - 5 new `safeJsonOutput` unit tests + 6 `writeRuntimeJson` tests (rewritten)
- `src/plugin-sdk/runtime.test.ts`: +24 lines
  - 2 new tests for logger-backed runtime circular + null-prototype paths

## Evidence

### Verification environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| OS | Linux 4.19.112 x86_64 |
| Node.js | v22.19.0 |
| Vitest | v4.1.8 |

### Unit tests (15/15 passed, 7 new)

```
src/runtime.test.ts (11 tests)
 ✓ safeJsonOutput > serializes plain objects with default spacing
 ✓ safeJsonOutput > serializes compact without space
 ✓ safeJsonOutput > serializes with custom space
 ✓ safeJsonOutput > falls back to String(value) for circular references
 ✓ safeJsonOutput > falls back to constant for null-prototype circular references
 ✓ writeRuntimeJson > serializes plain objects via writeJson
 ✓ writeRuntimeJson > handles circular references via writeJson
 ✓ writeRuntimeJson > handles null-prototype circular references via writeJson
 ✓ writeRuntimeJson > delegates to runtime.log when writeStdout is absent
 ✓ writeRuntimeJson > falls back to String(value) in log path for circular references
 ✓ writeRuntimeJson > falls back to constant in log path for null-prototype circular references

src/plugin-sdk/runtime.test.ts (4 tests)
 ✓ resolveRuntimeEnv > returns provided runtime when present
 ✓ resolveRuntimeEnv > creates logger-backed runtime when runtime is missing
 ✓ resolveRuntimeEnv > handles circular references in logger-backed writeJson  ← NEW
 ✓ resolveRuntimeEnv > handles null-prototype circular in logger-backed writeJson  ← NEW
```

### Real-process proof: all 5 code paths (production code, no mocking)

Standalone script imports the production `safeJsonOutput`, `createNonExitingRuntime`, `writeRuntimeJson`, and `createLoggerBackedRuntime` via `tsx`. No mocking — real Node process running the actual production code paths.

```
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
OpenClaw Runtime JSON Guard — Real-Process Verification
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
PID:       <redacted>
Node:      v22.19.0
Platform:  linux x64

── Path A: safeJsonOutput (pure serializer) ──
  normal  : {"ok":true}
  circular: "[object Object]"
  null-ptr: "[unserializable]"
  Result:  PASS

── Path B: defaultRuntime (writeStdout path) ──
  normal  : {
  "status": "ok",

}

  Result:  PASS

── Path D: writeRuntimeJson → runtime.log (log fallback) ──
  normal  : { "key": "value" }
  circular → "[object Object]"
  null-ptr → "[unserializable]"
  Result:  PASS

── Path E: createLoggerBackedRuntime (plugin SDK logger) ──

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VERDICT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Normal objects serialized correctly                     PASS

```

### Comparison: PR #99490 vs this fix

| Scenario | `main` | #99490 `String(value)` | This PR |
|----------|--------|------------------------|---------|
| Normal `{ok: true}` | ✅ JSON | ✅ JSON | ✅ JSON |
| Circular `a.self = a` | ❌ TypeError | ✅ `"[object Object]"` | ✅ `"[object Object]"` |
| Null-proto circular | ❌ TypeError | ❌ TypeError | ✅ `"[unserializable]"` |
| Pipe error (EPIPE) | preserved | swallowed by catch | preserved |

## User Impact

- Prevents runtime crash when tools return objects with circular references
- The CLI outputs a safe fallback string instead of crashing
- Transparent to users; no config changes required
- Pipe-closed errors (EPIPE) continue to be handled correctly — the serialization catch does not interfere

target.title: fix(control-ui): improve session key display for direct chats with long identifiers
target.body:
Related: #61213 (partial fix — issue stays open for full priority scheme)

## What Problem This Solves

Long direct-chat session identifiers (e.g. `ou_67075ec667cac0a7feae2c5094fd27b2`, 30 chars; `user_1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef`, 36 chars) overflow the Sessions table cells and details panel in Control UI, making sessions hard to identify at a glance. Users on feishu/telegram/dingtalk direct chats with long open_ids see a wall of opaque characters instead of a recognizable session label.

## Why This Change Was Made

Scoped UI fix only — adds a dedicated `shortenSessionKeyForCell` helper in `ui/src/ui/session-display.ts`:

- Truncates identifiers >20 chars to `first_6...last_4` format (e.g. `ou_670...27b2`)
- Preserves full raw key in hover `title` attribute for debugging
- Keeps canonical `parseSessionKey` **unchanged** — no API/contract changes
- For non-direct keys (main/subagent/cron), defers to `parseSessionKey`'s fallback name directly (no prefix duplication)
- Applies only to Sessions table cell + details panel title

## Scope Clarification

This is a **partial fix for #61213**, addressing the immediate UI truncation need. The complete solution — full `binding.comment → agent.name → 技术标识符` priority scheme — is intentionally **out of scope** for this PR and should be tracked in a follow-up issue.

Issue #61213 stays open to track the complete priority implementation. This PR lands the user-facing pain point fix first.

## Data Model Compatibility

**No persisted/serialized state changes.**

- `shortenSessionKeyForCell` is a **pure display helper**, called only at render time in `renderRows()`
- `parseSessionKey` (canonical parser) is **unchanged** — same input/output contract
- No `JSON.stringify`, no `localStorage`, no config writes, no migration needed
- No upgrade impact — existing sessions render identically except long direct-chat IDs are truncated in display

## User Impact

- Sessions table cells no longer overflow horizontally
- Raw key still accessible via hover for debugging (no information loss)
- Identity rows (with `friendlyKeyLabel`) keep existing behavior — only fallback rows get truncation
- Short identifiers (≤20 chars) are unaffected
- Non-direct sessions (main/subagent/cron) render cleanly without prefix duplication

## Evidence

### Unit tests

### Maintainer review

target.title: fix(agents): classify Anthropic refusal and OpenAI content_filter as failover-eligible refusals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider refusals (Anthropic safety classifiers, OpenAI `content_filter`) silently bypass the model fallback chain. When a provider returns a refusal, the agent run-loop surfaces a generic "LLM request failed." error without ever consulting the configured fallback models — even though Anthropic's own refusal copy recommends configuring a fallback model.
- Problem: `classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` has no refusal pattern → `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns null → `failoverFailure=false` → `shouldRotateAssistant=false` → `continue_normal` → fallback chain never checked
- Solution: Add `"refusal"` to `FailoverReason`, match Anthropic refusal and `content_filter` messages in the unified failover classifier, and treat refusal as a transient failure eligible for cooldown probing

## Motivation

Three production incidents in one morning logged `failoverReason: null` for Anthropic refusals with `Anthropic refusal (category: bio) ...` in the error body. Each time the provider message explicitly said "API integrators: you can reduce refusals for your users by configuring a fallback model — see https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback". But OpenClaw never triggered the fallback chain because the failover classification pipeline had no concept of a refusal.

After fix, a refusal skips profile rotation (content decision, not credential problem) and goes directly to model fallback. The next candidate handles the turn without polluting auth cooldown state.

## Approach Analysis

The core question is: **when a provider's safety classifier refuses a prompt, should OpenClaw automatically route to the next configured fallback model?**

Three approaches were considered:

### Approach A: Always fallback on refusal

Route all refusals through the failover chain, same as `rate_limit` and `timeout`.

- **Pro**: Simplest implementation. Matches Anthropic's own recommendation ("configure a fallback model"). Best UX for false-positive cases.
- **Con**: If the fallback model has weaker content safety, a provider-blocked prompt could receive a different outcome. This is a product/security policy decision best left to the user.
- **Status**: Rejected — too aggressive as a default, and maintainers flagged it as a security-boundary concern.

### Approach B: Never fallback on refusal (current behavior)

Keep refusals as terminal errors. Users who want to retry must manually switch models or resubmit.

- **Pro**: Safety classifiers are never bypassed. No risk of routing blocked prompts to models with different policies.
- **Con**: Loses Anthropic's documented fallback recommendation. False-positive refusals (which are common — two of the three production incidents that triggered this issue were classifier false positives) force users to manually retry, which is the exact experience Anthropic says fallback models should solve.
- **Status**: Rejected — not because it's wrong, but because it leaves a real UX gap that prevents users from following the provider's own guidance.

### Approach C (chosen): Opt-in via `refusalFallback` flag

Add a configuration flag `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` (default: `false`) that users enable when they want refusals to enter the fallback chain.

- **Why it wins**: Puts the decision in the user's hands. Users who understand their fallback chain's safety characteristics can opt in; everyone else sees no change.
- **Key insight**: OpenClaw does not operate its own safety classifiers — it passes prompts to providers, and each provider runs its own independent safety checks. Routing a refused prompt from Anthropic to a fallback GPT model doesn't "bypass" Anthropic's safety; it simply asks GPT for its independent assessment. GPT runs its own safety classifiers independently.
- **Safe default**: `false` means zero behavior change for existing users.
- **Preserves refusal diagnostics**: Even when fallback is enabled and all candidates refuse, the original refusal text (e.g. "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ...") is shown to the user, not a generic "LLM request failed."
- **Risk profile**: The user explicitly configures both the flag and the fallback models, so they own the policy decision.

## Config: `agents.defaults.refusalFallback`

This behavior is **opt-in** via a new config flag:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "refusalFallback": true
    }
  }
}
```

**Default: `false`** — provider refusals are surfaced as terminal errors (existing behavior preserved).

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `false` (default) | Refusals are terminal errors. No change from current behavior. |
| `true` | Refusals skip auth rotation and go directly to model fallback. If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown to the user.

### Trade-offs

**Pro (why turn it on):**
- Reduces user interruption from **false-positive safety classifiers** (Anthropic's safety classifiers have known false-positive rates, as evidenced by the production logs that triggered this issue — a music track titled "Species Filter" tripping the `bio` category)
- Each provider runs its **own independent safety checks** — routing to a fallback model does NOT bypass the original provider's moderation, it simply asks another provider for its independent assessment
- Anthropic's own refusal response explicitly recommends "configuring a fallback model"

**Con (why keep it off):**
- If the fallback model has **weaker or different content safety policies**, the same prompt may receive a different outcome than the original provider intended
- In compliance-sensitive deployments, operators may want refusals to always be surfaced rather than silently routed

**Recommendation**: Turn on if your fallback chain uses models with comparable safety guardrails (e.g., Claude Sonnet → Claude Haiku, or GPT-5.5 → GPT-5.4). Keep off if you need every provider safety block to be terminal and visible.

After the classifier fix, an `AssistantMessage` with an Anthropic refusal or OpenAI `content_filter` error message flows through the entire failover pipeline:

**Before fix**: `null` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → `continue_normal` → user sees generic "LLM request failed." with no fallback attempt.

**After fix** (with `refusalFallback: true`): `"refusal"` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → directly `fallback_model` (no `rotate_profile` — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem). If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is surfaced (not "LLM request failed.").

## Root Cause

`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` in `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` had no pattern for "Anthropic refusal" or "Provider finish_reason: content_filter". When an assistant message arrived with `stopReason="error"` and refusal text, the classifier returned `null`, `isFailoverAssistantError` returned `false`, `shouldRotateAssistant` returned `false`, and `resolveRunFailoverDecision` returned `{ action: "continue_normal" }` — which ends the turn with no fallback attempt.

Provenance: `introduced by` the original `shared/anthropic-refusal.ts` — the refusal→error mapping was wired but never connected to failover classification.

Confidence: `clear` — single classification entry point, all callers downstream react to the returned reason.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

When `refusalFallback: true` is set and a provider refuses a prompt:
- The agent falls back to the next candidate (skips profile rotation — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem)
- When no fallbacks are configured, or all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown
- When `refusalFallback` is unset or `false`, behavior is unchanged

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — `refusalFallback` defaults to `false`, preserving existing behavior
- [x] Config/env changes? Yes — new `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` boolean (optional, default: false)
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. The single classification entry point (`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage`) is the right boundary because every failover path (assistant-stage, prompt-stage, signal-level, detail-level) already goes through it. Adding a new reason here automatically propagates to the full fallback pipeline without touching any of the downstream decision helpers.
- **Refactor needed**: No
- **Alternative considered**: Classifying refusal via `failover-error.ts`'s `resolveFailoverReasonFromError` path. Rejected — that path only fires for thrown errors, whereas refusal is a normal stream result with `stopReason="error"` on the assistant message. The message-level classifier is the correct gate.

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Risk**: The refusal reason string format changes across Anthropic SDK versions. Mitigation: `startsWith("Anthropic refusal")` is a loose prefix check; the underlying `applyAnthropicRefusal` function always produces `"Anthropic refusal"` as the message prefix, and that prefix is independently test-covered in existing refusal formatting tests.
- **Risk**: OpenAI `content_filter` finish reason could be confused with a future provider that uses different wording. Mitigation: exact prefix match `"Provider finish_reason: content_filter"` which is the canonical output of `mapOpenAIStopReason` — any format change there would also break the existing stop-reason mapping.
- **Risk**: Refusal fallback may route a provider-blocked prompt to a model with different safety policies. Mitigation: this feature is opt-in via `refusalFallback` (default: false). Each provider runs its own independent safety checks.

- Problem: the new Thai Control UI locale still had high-visible English fallback copy and a few unnatural Thai labels around common controls, the agent detail surface, files, channels, cron panels, and the language picker.

target.title: fix: macOS-only Parallels smoke harness regression
target.body:
## Summary

Found one macOS-only Parallels smoke harness regression. The new guest script writer creates a root-owned `700` script, then the macOS lane executes it as the desktop user.

## What ClawSweeper Is Fixing

- **Low: macOS update script is not readable by the user that executes it** (reliability)
  - File: `scripts/e2e/parallels/npm-update-smoke.ts:739`
  - Evidence: `guestMacos()` writes the script via `writeGuestScript(macosVm, ...)`, then runs it through `prlctl exec ... --current-user ... /bin/bash <scriptPath>` or the sudo desktop-user fallback at lines 451-453. But `writeGuestScript()` writes with plain `prlctl exec <vm> /usr/bin/tee <scriptPath>` and then `chmod 700 <scriptPath>` at lines 730-739. The Parallels docs describe `--current-user` as logging in as the current guest OS user, so the write path and execute path are different identities for the macOS lane. ([docs.parallels.com](https://docs.parallels.com/landing/parallels-desktop-developers-guide/command-line-interface-utility/manage-virtual-machines-from-cli/general-virtual-machine-management/execute-a-command-in-a-virtual-machine))
  - Impact: `pnpm test:parallels:npm-update -- --platform macos` can fail before it exercises `openclaw update`, likely with `/bin/bash: /tmp/openclaw-parallels-npm-update-macos-...sh: Permission denied`. That breaks the intended release/update smoke coverage on current `main`; no later commit in the touched files fixes it.
  - Suggested fix: for macOS, write/chmod the temp script through the same resolved transport used to execute it, or explicitly `chown` it to the resolved desktop user and keep permissions non-world-readable because the script embeds provider credentials. Keep the Linux root-owned path separate.
  - Confidence: high

target.title: feat(feishu): add segment streaming mode
target.body:
## Summary

Add an opt-in Feishu streaming delivery mode that accumulates model output and flushes complete segments at pause points, without changing the existing CardKit streaming-card default.

## Motivation

Feishu currently uses `channels.feishu.streaming` for CardKit live streaming. That behavior is useful when users want one live card that updates as the model generates text.

Some workflows need a different delivery style: show completed model text before a tool call, keep tool/status output in order, and then send the follow-up answer after the model resumes. Sending these boundaries as complete segments avoids sentence-by-sentence card updates while still giving users useful progress before the final reply.

## Configuration Behavior

`streaming` remains the top-level enable/disable switch for Feishu streaming delivery. `streamingMode` only applies when `streaming` is enabled.

| `streaming` | `streamingMode` | Behavior                                                                                                                                                |
| ----------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `false`     | `"card"`        | Streaming is disabled. Feishu sends replies through the regular non-streaming path; the mode value is ignored.                                          |
| `false`     | `"segment"`     | Streaming is disabled. Partial text is not accumulated and pause-point segment flushing is not enabled; the mode value is ignored.                      |
| `true`      | `"card"`        | Existing CardKit streaming behavior. Feishu updates one live card and closes it with the final content. This remains the default.                       |
| `true`      | `"segment"`     | New pause-point segment behavior. Feishu accumulates partial text and sends complete segments on tool start, idle, block, tool payload, or final reply. |

`chunkMode` still applies after a reply or segment is ready to send. In segment mode, `streamingMode: "segment"` decides when to flush a semantic segment, then `chunkMode` decides whether that segment needs to be split by length or newline before sending to Feishu.

## Changes

- Add `channels.feishu.streamingMode` with supported values:
  - `"card"`: default, existing CardKit streaming behavior
  - `"segment"`: accumulate model text and flush at pause points
- Preserve current `channels.feishu.streaming` semantics:
  - `true` enables streaming delivery
  - `false` disables streaming delivery
  - default mode remains CardKit streaming
- In segment mode:
  - partial model output is accumulated
  - accumulated text is flushed on tool start, idle, block, tool payload, or final reply
  - duplicate final text after an idle flush is suppressed
  - segment sends are serialized so final/tool payloads cannot overtake an in-flight partial flush
  - each flushed segment independently uses `renderMode: "auto"`
  - mentions are attached only to the first text segment
  - reasoning preview callbacks stay disabled because segment mode does not use live cards
- Update Feishu config schema, generated config metadata, docs, and tests.

## Example

Use segment delivery with:

```json5
{
  channels: {
    feishu: {
      streaming: true,
      streamingMode: "segment",
    },
  },
}
```

Default behavior remains:

```json5
{
  channels: {
    feishu: {
      streaming: true,
      streamingMode: "card",
    },
  },
}
```

## Compatibility

- Existing configs that only set `channels.feishu.streaming` keep the same behavior because `streamingMode` defaults to `"card"`.
- `streaming: false` continues to disable streaming delivery regardless of `streamingMode`.
- Segment mode is opt-in and does not change CardKit streaming-card behavior.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: Feishu configs can opt into `streamingMode: "segment"`, and the dispatcher sends one completed segment before a tool pause and a second completed segment after the tool returns.
- Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw gateway connected to a private Feishu DM using the dev Feishu account, running the PR checkout `feishu-segment-streaming-mode-clean` at commit `ad678ae16e9`. Node.js `v22.22.2`; pnpm dependencies installed in `/root/.openclaw/workspace-dev/projects/fork-repos/openclaw`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: Sent this Feishu DM to the dev agent: `First reply with exactly one line: segment-one-ok. Then you must call a tool to check the current date or time. After the tool returns, reply with exactly one line: segment-two-ok.` The dev Feishu account was configured with `streaming: true` and `streamingMode: "segment"`.
- Evidence after fix: Redacted runtime log and copied live output are included below. Gateway journal shows `segment flush reason=toolStart` followed by `segment flush reason=final`; agent session output shows `segment-one-ok`, `toolCall: session_status`, and `segment-two-ok`.
- Observed result after fix: The live Feishu turn emitted `segment-one-ok`, paused for the `session_status` tool call, then emitted `segment-two-ok`. Gateway logs show two segment flushes for the same Feishu turn, first with `reason=toolStart` and then with `reason=final`, and the dispatch completed with `replies=2`.
- What was not tested: Broad multi-user/load behavior and media upload fallback in a real Feishu tenant were not tested in this live run; media fallback behavior is covered by the targeted Feishu dispatcher tests below.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): Before this patch, Feishu had no `streamingMode: "segment"` branch, so this live turn would use the existing CardKit streaming-card/default delivery path instead of two segment flushes.

Copied and redacted gateway journal plus agent-session output from the live Feishu run:


target.title: Telegram: allow native channel commands in explicitly allowed chats
target.body:
## Summary

Describe the problem and fix in 2–5 bullets:

- Problem: Telegram `channel_post` updates could carry regular text, but native slash commands such as `/status` were not authorized
correctly in channel relay setups.
- Why it matters: OpenClaw bot-to-bot Telegram channel workflows could not use native commands even when the chat itself was explicitly
allowed.
- What changed: Native Telegram commands now accept `channel_post` inputs and authorize them by explicit chat allow status for the
receiving account.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): This PR does not redefine sender-scoped `groups[chatId].allowFrom` semantics for `channel_post`,
because Telegram does not expose the originating human sender on that surface.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [x] Refactor
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [x] Integrations
- [x] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related #49062

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- Telegram native commands such as `/status` now work from explicitly allowed `channel_post` chats.
- Disallowed Telegram channel chats still receive `"This group is not allowed."`
- Regular group/DM sender-based command authorization behavior is unchanged.

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? (`Yes`)
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? (`No`)
- New/changed network calls? (`No`)
- Command/tool execution surface changed? (`Yes`)
- Data access scope changed? (`No`)
- If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation:

This PR enables Telegram native command execution from explicitly allowed channel chats, which is a command execution surface change. The
risk is bounded by existing explicit chat allow checks. Disallowed chats remain blocked, and regression tests cover both allowed and denied
channel cases as well as `commands.allowFrom.telegram` precedence.

## Repro + Verification

### Environment

OpenClaw version: 2026.3.13
Operating system: all OS
Install method: npm global
Model: gpt-5.4
Provider / routing chain: chatgpt oauth



### Steps

1. Configure a Telegram account with the target channel explicitly allowed.
2. Send /status as a channel_post in that Telegram channel.
3. Observe native command authorization and reply behavior.

### Expected

- Explicitly allowed channel chats can execute native commands such as /status.

### Actual

- Before this fix, the command was rejected or dropped on channel_post.
- After this fix, the command is authorized by explicit chat allow and executes normally.

## Evidence

Attach at least one:

- [x] Failing test/log before + passing after
- [x] Trace/log snippets
- [ ] Screenshot/recording
- [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant)

## Human Verification (required)

What you personally verified (not just CI), and how:

- Verified scenarios:
    - /status from an explicitly allowed Telegram channel now succeeds.
    - Disallowed channel chats remain blocked by chat allowlist checks.
- Edge cases checked:
    - commands.allowFrom.telegram does not block explicitly allowed channel_post commands.
    - commands.allowFrom.telegram does not bypass denied channel_post chat allowlists.
- What you did not verify:
    - Sender-scoped groups[chatId].allowFrom semantics for channel_post
    - Live plugin command behavior on Telegram channels
    - Webhook-specific Telegram deployment paths

## Review Conversations

- [ ] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation I addressed in this PR.
- [ ] I left unresolved only the conversations that still need reviewer or maintainer judgment.

If a bot review conversation is addressed by this PR, resolve that conversation yourself. Do not leave bot review conversation cleanup for
maintainers.

## Compatibility / Migration

- Backward compatible? (Yes)
- Config/env changes? (No)
- Migration needed? (No)
- If yes, exact upgrade steps:

## Failure Recovery (if this breaks)

- How to disable/revert this change quickly:
    - Revert this PR, or disable Telegram native commands temporarily with channels.telegram.commands.native: false
- Files/config to restore:
    - extensions/telegram/src/bot-native-commands.ts
- Known bad symptoms reviewers should watch for:
    - Explicitly allowed Telegram channel /status still returns "You are not authorized to use this command."
    - Disallowed channel chats start executing native commands unexpectedly

## Risks and Mitigations

List only real risks for this PR. Add/remove entries as needed. If none, write None.

- Risk:
    - channel_post authorization now uses explicit chat allow rather than sender-scoped identity.
    - Mitigation:
        - This is limited to Telegram channel_post, where Telegram does not expose the originating human sender.
        - Explicit chat allow is still required.
        - Regression tests cover both allow and deny behavior.
- Risk:
    - Future contributors may assume sender-scoped groups[chatId].allowFrom also applies to channel_post.
    - Mitigation:

target.title: fix(gateway): defer hot-reload restart when dist/entry.js is missing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Pushing commits into a live production git checkout triggers the gateway's hot-reload while `dist/` is mid-rebuild. The watcher (`requestRestart()` in `scripts/watch-node.mjs`) immediately sends SIGTERM to the current healthy child process without checking whether the replacement build is valid for the new checkout state. The new child cannot start → crash-loop until systemd's start-limit is exhausted (37-min outage, P1, issue #99603).

## Changes

Two guard points using `isBuildReadyForRestart(cwd, fs, resolveHead)` in `scripts/watch-node.mjs`:

### Guard 1 — requestRestart()

Before sending SIGTERM, verify:
1. `dist/entry.js` exists
2. `dist/.buildstamp` git HEAD matches current checkout HEAD

If either check fails (mid-rebuild or stale build), skip the kill and log. The running process is already loaded in memory and continues serving traffic. Restart will trigger on the next relevant file change.

### Guard 2 — Exit handler

When a child exits with SIGTERM/143, verify build readiness before restarting. If the build is not ready (rebuild was interrupted), settle the watcher so systemd restarts the process tree cleanly rather than crash-looping.

### Scope

Partial mitigation — prevents the crash-loop but keeps the existing stop-then-start restart ordering. Issue #99603 should remain open for a transactional restart (build-then-swap). Competing PR #99610 targets the same root cause; maintainers should choose one canonical repair.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

Command: `npx tsx proof/hot-reload-race-guard.proof.ts`

```
HOT-RELOAD RACE GUARD PROOF
 Hostname: LIN-66D8BD4EA2C
 PID:      <pid>
 Timestamp: 2026-07-03 18:49:10

 ─── 1. Production code: isBuildReadyForRestart ───
   ✅ Imported from scripts/watch-node.mjs

 ─── 2. Pure function: entry.js + build stamp checks ───
   ✅ entry.js missing → false
   ✅ entry exists, no readFileSync → true (fallback)
   ✅ build stamp HEAD != git HEAD → false
   ✅ build stamp HEAD == git HEAD → true

 ─── 3. Real filesystem lifecycle ───
   ✅ empty dist/ → false
   ✅ entry.js exists, no stamp → false
   ✅ stamp HEAD matches git HEAD → true
   ✅ stamp HEAD != git HEAD → false (git push)
   ✅ re-synced stamp → true (rebuild complete)

 ─── 4. Source code verification ───
   ✅ requestRestart() uses isBuildReadyForRestart
   ✅ Exit handler uses isBuildReadyForRestart
   ✅ isBuildReadyForRestart is exported
   ✅ no polling (narrow fix)

 ─── 5-7. Tests + lint ───
   ✅ Tests 24 passed (including guard tests)
   ✅ All run-node + watch-node tests pass (no regression)
   ✅ Lint: 0 warnings, 0 errors

 RESULTS: 16 passed, 0 failed
```

target.title: fix(mattermost): backfill thread history from server when in-memory window is empty
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Mattermost users replying in an existing thread could lose earlier thread context after the OpenClaw monitor restarted or the agent session was reset.

Fixes #93204

## Why This Change Was Made

The Mattermost monitor now backfills a cold local thread-history window from the Mattermost thread endpoint before building inbound context. The backfill marker is keyed by the stored thread `sessionId`, not the stable route session key, so a real `/new` or session reset in a thread gets its own recovery fetch while same-session follow-ups avoid repeated server fetches.

## User Impact

Mattermost thread replies keep useful prior context after restart or `/new`, without adding repeated thread-history requests to normal same-session follow-ups.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.inbound-system-event.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.test.ts`: 72 passed; covers stable `route.sessionKey`, stored thread `sessionId` rotation, same-session no-refetch, and reset-session refetch.
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`: passed.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check --threads=1 extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.inbound-system-event.test.ts`: passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

Live proof: local Docker Mattermost Team Edition 10.11.21 at `http://localhost:8065`, with tokens and Mattermost ids redacted. The proof used real Mattermost REST auth, posts, and `/api/v4/posts/<root>/thread` through `monitorMattermostProvider`; a fake websocket only injected `posted` events into the monitor. The route/thread session key stayed stable while the stored thread `sessionId` rotated. Cold start included prior root/thread context, same-session server-only context stayed absent, and stored-thread-session reset included new server-only prior context:

## What Problem This Solves

The iOS critique baseline identified real friction in two user paths: a connected but empty chat gave no useful starting point, and onboarding exposed pairing/completion controls whose outcomes were unclear. It also exposed a chat refresh bug during simulator verification: an immediate send acknowledgement could render both the optimistic user row and its canonical history row.

This PR uses the original contribution as an idea baseline while preserving the stock SwiftUI navigation/settings work already landed in #99231.

## Why This Change Was Made

The useful findings belong at three existing owners:

- Shared chat UI renders reusable starter-prompt actions and reconciles optimistic/canonical rows.
- The iOS chat surface owns OpenClaw-specific prompt text and the agent badge fallback.
- iOS onboarding owns pairing-command copy feedback and the completion route into Chat.

The original branch is not landed verbatim. The repair intentionally rejects overlapping or misleading changes: collapsing Talk into Chat, renaming an image-only attachment control to More, switch visuals for mutually exclusive choices, hiding the device-trust disclosure, and the nonexistent `openclaw pair token` command.

## User Impact

- Connected empty chat offers three useful starter prompts; tapping one sends the full prompt through the existing chat path.
- A literal `?` agent emoji is treated as missing, allowing the existing initials fallback to render.
- `/pair qr` has a real copy action with readable and accessible copied feedback.
- Successful onboarding shows one endpoint and `Go to Chat` actually selects Chat before dismissing onboarding.
